candidates.title: edit's fuzzy replacers run quadratic pure-Python matching on the event loop inside the writer transaction, with no size, count or time bound
candidates.description: Any principal that may edit one file, including its own, can send an edit whose old string misses exactly. The router then falls back to the fuzzy replacers in src/vfs/storage/replace.py, and three of them are quadratic. block_anchor_replacer scans from every first-anchor line to the end of the file, so it is O(L^2) in lines. It also runs a full-matrix pure-Python Levenshtein, O(M^2) in line length. line_trimmed_replacer pays O(L^2) through its per-match prefix sums and the per-match context split. edit_rows calls this code synchronously in the coroutine. It runs once per target, inside the SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE writer transaction. No cap applies to old/new length, the number of edits, the number of targets, or wall time. One small call therefore freezes the host's event loop for every agent sharing the process, and it holds the mount's write lock the whole time. Measured: a 16 KB file with a 5-byte old string blocked the loop for 1.08 s; a 2 KB file with a 2 KB old string blocked it for 0.74 s. Each doubling of input costs about 4x, and the cost multiplies by the number of targets.
candidates.root_cause: replace() falls back to the fuzzy replacers whenever the exact search misses. block_anchor_replacer's forward scan has no exit when the last anchor is absent, levenshtein is a full O(n*m) Python matrix with no length cap, and line_trimmed/replace recompute offsets and context per match. edit_rows runs edited_entry inline in the async writer transaction for every target, with no offload, deadline or input caps.
candidates.intended_behavior: An edit's matching cost should be bounded: near-linear in content and old_string size, with fuzzy fallback refused or capped above a declared work budget. CPU-bound matching should leave the event loop the way grep verify and reindex do (call_offloaded with a deadline), and should finish before the writer lock is taken, or at least without holding it unbounded, so one caller cannot stall other principals.

conditions.description: The caller needs edit (modify) rights on at least one text entry, for example a file it wrote itself. No rights over other principals' data are needed.

The host process serves several agents or principals from one event loop and mount (the embedded-library model). The writer-lock effect applies to SQLite-backed mounts; on other engines the loop stall remains.

The target's content and the old string are shaped to miss exactly and reach a quadratic fuzzy path: many lines equal to the first anchor with the last anchor absent, a long differing middle line, or many whitespace-trimmed matches.

remediation.strategy:
Bound the work and move it off the loop. (1) In block_anchor_replacer, precompute the indices of last-anchor lines once and find the next one by bisect, which removes the O(L^2) scan. Compute line start offsets once with a prefix sum and use them in both fuzzy replacers. Cap the context listed in the multi-match error at a few matches. (2) Replace the Python levenshtein with a banded or early-exit version, or a vfs-core kernel, and skip fuzzy similarity when a middle line exceeds a declared length or len(content_lines)*len(find_lines) exceeds a work budget. Refuse with a classified invalid error that names the exact-match requirement. (3) Run edited_entry for the batch through call_offloaded with a deadline, before or outside the writer transaction where the version guard already makes that safe. Regression test: count calls to str.strip or levenshtein cells, never wall time, for the 'a
'*L / 'a
x
b' shape at L and 2L, and assert linear growth.

likelihood.reason: Any principal with edit rights on any one file, including its own, can trigger it with a few-KB request. Agents routinely issue edits whose old string misses, and nothing upstream in params.py, base.py or the storage caps old/new length, edit count or target count.

impact.reason: The stall freezes the shared event loop for every other principal on the host, and on SQLite it holds the mount's writer lock for a time quadratic in input. 16 KB gave about 1 s; extrapolated at the measured 4x per doubling, 64 KB gives about 17 s. The effect is transient (ends when the call ends), leaves no persistent state, and repeats per call.

confidence.reason: The quadratic loops are plain in source. The growth (about 4x per doubling), the loop stall and the blocked read by a different principal were all observed through the public verb at three sizes per shape.

candidates.title: markdown_refs folds the whole enclosing line for every reference, so one agent-written markdown line makes reindex hold the mount's writer transaction for quadratic time
candidates.description: During reindex, the chunk pass parses every dirty markdown body with the Rust markdown_refs. For each link destination or path-shaped code span it calls line_context. That function scans back to the previous newline and forward to the next one, then folds the whole line, before it keeps 256 characters. So N references on one line of length ~N cost O(N^2). The pass is offloaded to a thread, so the event loop keeps running. But it runs inside chunk_dirty's writer transaction (BEGIN IMMEDIATE on SQLite), with no time or size budget. Every other principal's write on that mount waits for the whole parse. An agent that writes one 160 KB single-line markdown file makes the next operator reindex take 6.8 s instead of about 0.5 s, and other writers on the mount block for 6.5 s. Each doubling of the line costs about 3.5-4x. The stall repeats on every reindex after the agent rewrites the file.
candidates.root_cause: line_context (crates/vfs-core/src/links.rs:71-75) recomputes the line bounds and folds the entire line per reference, rather than once per line or within a window bounded by MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS. extract_link_work runs inside _assess_and_split, awaited while chunk_dirty's writer transaction is open (indexing.py:330, backend.py:1375), with no deadline or per-body work cap.
candidates.intended_behavior: The reference extraction should be linear in body size, with a per-reference context cost bounded by MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS. Reindex CPU over caller-written content should be bounded or should run without the mount's writer lock held, so one document cannot block other principals' writes for superlinear time.

conditions.description: The attacker needs write rights to any one .md path on the mount, for example its own file.
The trusted operator or host runs reindex on the mount (the routine maintenance verb that fills indexes and vectors); agents cannot call it themselves.

Other principals write to the same mount while reindex runs. The writer-lock effect is direct on SQLite and InMemoryStorage; on server engines the transaction holds row locks from the stale-flag UPDATE only, so the shared effect there was not measured.

execution.attacker_perspective: A named agent principal (alice) writes one markdown file to a shared mount; the operator later runs storage.reindex(); another principal (bob) writes his own file during the reindex.
payloads: control: write /doc.md content='[a](b.md)\n' * 16000 (same bytes and refs on 16000 lines)
native split: markdown_refs([b'`a.md` ' * N]) versus markdown_refs([b'`a b` ' * N])
instructions: Run agents/w2d-reindex-edit/scratch/reindex_scale.py and md_rootcause.py under tools/sandbox-run.py (no network, empty env, CPU 60 s, wall 120 s, RSS 2 GiB) with .venv/bin/python -I.

For N=4000, 8000 and 16000 on a fresh InMemoryStorage, time reindex(). Record bob's concurrent write latency, a rival reindex() outcome and the longest event-loop gap. Repeat N=16000 on a file-backed SQLite DatabaseStorage.
execution.observed_result: InMemoryStorage one-line: reindex 559 / 1864 / 6819 ms at N=4000/8000/16000 (x3.34, x3.66). bob's write waited 218 / 1509 / 6478 ms; the event-loop gap stayed at most 85 ms; the rival reindex got vfs.conflict. Control on N lines: 165 ms (N=4000), 533 ms (N=16000), bob's write 7-188 ms. File SQLite N=16000: reindex 6722 ms, and bob's write on a separate pooled connection waited 6463 ms. Native split: path-shaped spans 1146 -> 4458 ms (x3.89) versus non-path spans 41.6 -> 84.4 ms (x2.03).

remediation.strategy: Make the context cost per reference O(MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS). One way: compute the newline offsets once per body with memchr, and find each reference's line by binary search. Because references come in document order, cache the folded context per line start, so each line is folded once and early-exits after MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS output chars. Separately, consider a per-body reference cap or time budget for the extraction, and doing the offloaded CPU before the writer transaction opens, since the chunked flip is already version-guarded. Regression test: count fold_line invocations or bytes scanned, never wall time, for one line with N and 2N references, and assert linear growth.

likelihood.reason: Writing one markdown file is ordinary agent capability, and reindex is routine operator maintenance. The attacker cannot start reindex, but every reindex after each rewrite of the file pays the cost again.

impact.reason: All principals' writes on the mount block for a time quadratic in one file's line length: 6.5 s at 160 KB, and about 100 s extrapolated at 640 KB at the measured 3.5-4x per doubling. On file SQLite a writer blocked past about 4 x 5 s busy_timeout would fail with a conflict (inferred from source, not run). The event loop is not stalled, and the stall ends when the pass commits.

confidence.reason: The root cause is isolated by the native split (non-path spans with the same parse are linear). The end-to-end quadratic growth and the blocked concurrent writer were observed on InMemoryStorage and on file SQLite.

hardening: replace() builds its multi-match error from every match's line number and 7-line context (replace.py:321-333), so the returned error string grows linearly with match count (8000 matches for a 16 KB file); cap the listed matches at a small number.
levenshtein (replace.py:66) also allocates a full (n+1)x(m+1) Python list matrix, so memory is O(n*m) as well as time; a two-row implementation bounds the memory to O(m) even before a time cap.
fold_line (links.rs:78-92) folds the whole input before take(MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS); an early break after MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS output chars is cheap even after the per-line caching fix.

Because chunk_dirty processes the whole dirty set in one writer transaction, one expensive markdown body also delays chunking and link publishing for every other dirty entry in that pass (head-of-line); this is the same root cause, recorded under the line_context candidate.

The reindex single-runner lease refused a rival reindex with a retryable vfs.conflict during the long pass, as designed; with a pass longer than REINDEX_LEASE_TTL_MS (5 min), the heartbeat cannot land while the chunk pass holds SQLite's write lock (the backend docstring acknowledges this), so lease expiry during an attacker-lengthened pass is worth a deterministic test.
